Description: explicit — client-side hypsometric tint (color-relief layer, GL JS 5.6+)
prompt: I have terrain tiles as a raster-dem source in MapLibre GL JS and I want to color the map by elevation ranges (a hypsometric tint) directly client-side — blues at sea level through greens and browns to white peaks — without pre-rendering colored raster tiles. What layer type do I use and how do I configure the color ramp?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Short answer** *Use a **`color-relief`** layer.* It reads the same `raster-dem` source you already have and lets you paint the DEM directly with an `interpolate` expression over the special `["elevation"]` expression. The ramp you define inside the `color-relief-color` paint property is the hypsometric tint (blue → green → brown → white). Below is a complete, minimal example that you can drop into any MapLibre-GL-JS (v5.6 or newer) map. --- ## 1. Add the DEM source (if you haven’t already) ```js map.addSource('terrain-dem', { type: 'raster-dem', url: 'https://my.tileserver.com/terrain/{z}/{x}/{y}.webp', // or a TileJSON URL tileSize: 256, // default, keep it if you’re not sure maxzoom: 14, // whatever your DEM tiles support encoding: 'terrarium' // or 'mapbox' – must match the tiles you serve }); ``` > **Note** – The source is *only* a `raster-dem`. Do **not** add a `raster` layer for it; the > `color-relief` layer will do the drawing. --- ## 2. Add a `color-relief` layer that tints by elevation ```js map.addLayer({ id: 'hypsometric-tint', type: 'color-relief', // ← the layer type you need source: 'terrain-dem', // same source as above paint: { // The ramp – an interpolate expression over the special ["elevation"] value 'color-relief-color': [ 'interpolate', ['linear'], // linear interpolation between stops ['elevation'], // <-- only works inside color-relief-color // ── elevation (meters) ── ── colour ─────────────────────── 0, '#2c7bb6', // deep ocean – dark blue 50, '#3b8cc4', // shallow water – lighter blue 200, '#5fa5d0', // near-shore – cyan-green 500, '#a6d96a', // lowlands – bright green 1000, '#ffffbf', // foothills – yellow-ish 1500, '#fdae61', // mid-mountains – orange 2500, '#d73027', // high mountains – red-brown 3500, '#ffffff' // snow caps – white ], // Optional – make the tint semi-transparent so underlying imagery can still be seen 'color-relief-opacity': 0.85, // Optional – control how the DEM is sampled when the map is zoomed far out // (available from GL-JS 5.20). 'linear' is the default. // 'resampling': 'linear' } }); ``` ### How the ramp works | Elevation (m) | Hex colour | Visual cue | |---------------|------------|------------| | **0** | `#2c7bb6` | Deep ocean (dark blue) | | **50** | `#3b8cc4` | Shallow water (lighter blue) | | **200** | `#5fa5d0` | Near-shore (cyan-green) | | **500** | `#a6d96a` | Lowland vegetation (green) | | **1000** | `#ffffbf` | Foothills (yellow) | | **1500** | `#fdae61` | Mid-mountain (orange) | | **2500** | `#d73027` | High mountain (red-brown) | | **3500** | `#ffffff` | Snow caps (white) | *You can add, remove, or reorder stops to match the palette you want. The expression is evaluated **per-pixel** on the client, so the map updates instantly when you change the stops.* --- ## 3. (Optional) Keep 3-D terrain separate If you also want a 3-D mesh you can still call `map.setTerrain({source: 'terrain-dem', exaggeration: 1});`. The `color-relief` layer works **independently** of the terrain mesh – you can have both a hypsometric tint *and* a 3-D view at the same time. ```js map.setTerrain({ source: 'terrain-dem', exaggeration: 1 }); map.easeTo({ pitch: 60, bearing: 0, duration: 2000 }); ``` --- ## 4. Common pitfalls (so you don’t waste time) | Symptom | Why it happens | Fix | |---------|----------------|-----| | `["elevation"]` is “unknown property” | You placed the expression in a `raster` or `hillshade` layer, or outside `color-relief-color`. | Use a **`color-relief`** layer and keep the expression **inside** `color-relief-color`. | | The map stays gray/black | The source is a `raster` layer, not `raster-dem`, or the layer type is wrong. | Ensure the source type is `raster-dem` and the layer type is `color-relief`. | | Colors look washed out | You omitted opacity or used fully opaque white on top of imagery. | Adjust `color-relief-opacity` (e.g., `0.8`) or change the stop colours. | | No effect on the map | The style validator rejected the layer because you’re on an older MapLibre version (< 5.6). | Upgrade to the latest MapLibre-GL-JS (≥ 5.6). | | Performance drops on mobile | Very many stops or a very high-resolution DEM at high zoom. | Keep the ramp to ~8–12 stops; consider lowering `maxzoom` of the DEM source if you don’t need fine detail. | --- ## 5. Full minimal HTML/JS example (copy-paste ready) ```html Hypsometric tint with color-relief
``` Open the file in a browser, and you’ll see the DEM coloured exactly as defined by the ramp, without any pre-rendered coloured raster tiles. --- ### TL;DR * **Layer type:** `color-relief` * **Key paint property:** `color-relief-color` with an `interpolate` expression over `["elevation"]` * **Optional extras:** `color-relief-opacity`, `resampling` (GL JS 5.20+) That’s all you need to get a client-side hypsometric tint from a `raster-dem` source in MapLibre. Happy mapping!

Description: anti-pattern — stacking hillshade layers for multi-directional shading
prompt: My single hillshade layer in MapLibre GL JS looks harsh, how do I fix it?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### Why a Hillshade Can Look “Harsh” A **single** `hillshade` layer is already enough to give you a shaded-relief background. If the result is too contrasty (black shadows, white highlights, “chalky” ridges) the cause is almost always one of the following paint properties: | Property | What it does | Typical harsh-looking value | Softer alternative | |----------|--------------|----------------------------|--------------------| | `hillshade-method` | How the light is computed. | `standard` (default) – a single light source that can produce deep blacks and bright whites. | `multidirectional` (lights from several directions) or `igor` (minimises impact on underlying layers). | | `hillshade-exaggeration` | Scales the slope-derived shading. | `0.5` (default) – can be too strong on steep terrain. | `0.3-0.4` for a gentler look. | | `hillshade-illumination-anchor` | Where the light source is anchored. | `viewport` – the light stays fixed to the screen, which can make shadows look “flat” when you rotate the map. | `map` – the light rotates with the map, giving a more natural feel. | | `hillshade-shadow-color` / `hillshade-highlight-color` | Colours of shadows / highlights. | Opaque black (`#000000`) and white (`#FFFFFF`). | Add an alpha channel (e.g. `rgba(30,40,80,0.45)` for shadows, `rgba(255,240,200,0.4)` for highlights) and use cooler shadows / warmer highlights. | > **Do not stack multiple hillshade layers** to simulate multi-directional lighting. Since MapLibre GL JS 5.5 you can get the same effect with a single layer and the `hillshade-method` property, which is far cheaper performance-wise. --- ## Step-by-Step Fix 1. **Make sure you are using a recent MapLibre GL JS version** (≥ 5.5). The `hillshade-method` paint property was added in 5.5. 2. **Replace (or edit) your hillshade layer definition** with the softer settings below. You can copy-paste the JSON into your style or into the `addLayer` call you already have. ```json { "id": "hillshade", "type": "hillshade", "source": "terrain-dem", // <-- your raster-dem source name "paint": { // 1️⃣ Use a multi-directional light source (or "igor") "hillshade-method": "multidirectional", // 2️⃣ Reduce the overall contrast "hillshade-exaggeration": 0.35, // 3️⃣ Let the light rotate with the map (optional but often looks better) "hillshade-illumination-anchor": "map", // 4️⃣ Softer, semi-transparent colours "hillshade-shadow-color": "rgba(30,40,80,0.45)", "hillshade-highlight-color": "rgba(255,240,200,0.4)" } } ``` 3. **If you still need a little extra “softening”,** you can tweak the two colour alphas: ```js // Example: make shadows a bit lighter map.setPaintProperty('hillshade', 'hillshade-shadow-color', 'rgba(30,40,80,0.30)'); // Example: make highlights a touch warmer map.setPaintProperty('hillshade', 'hillshade-highlight-color', 'rgba(255,250,220,0.45)'); ``` 4. **Optional: Adjust illumination direction** (only matters for `standard`, `basic`, or `combined` methods). For `multidirectional` you can leave it at the default, but if you switch back to a single-direction method you might want: ```json "hillshade-illumination-direction": 315 // degrees clockwise from north ``` 5. **Refresh / re-render** the map (or just call `map.triggerRepaint()` if you changed paint properties programmatically). The hillshade should now look smoother and blend better with the imagery underneath. --- ## Quick Checklist | ✅ | Check | |---|-------| | **Version** | `maplibregl.version` ≥ 5.5 | | **Single layer** | Only one `type: "hillshade"` layer for the DEM | | **Method** | `hillshade-method: "multidirectional"` (or `"igor"`) | | **Exaggeration** | ≤ 0.4 (lower if still too strong) | | **Anchor** | `"map"` (optional, but avoids a static light) | | **Shadow / Highlight colours** | Use `rgba(..., alpha)` with α ≈ 0.3-0.5 | | **No extra hillshade layers** | Remove any duplicated hillshade layers that were added to “soften” the effect | --- ## What If It Still Looks Harsh? | Symptom | Likely cause | Fix | |---------|--------------|-----| | **Very dark valleys, almost black** | Shadow colour still opaque or `hillshade-exaggeration` too high | Lower `hillshade-exaggeration` further (e.g. 0.2) and increase shadow alpha (`rgba(...,0.2)`). | | **Bright “paper-white” ridges** | Highlight colour opaque | Reduce highlight alpha or switch to a warmer tint (`rgba(255,240,200,0.3)`). | | **Hard edges that look like a stencil** | Using `hillshade-method: "standard"` with default illumination direction | Switch to `"multidirectional"` or `"igor"`; they blend multiple light directions automatically. | | **Performance drop after changes** | You accidentally added multiple hillshade layers | Keep only one hillshade layer; remove the extras. | | **No change at all** | Your MapLibre version is older than 5.5 (no `hillshade-method` support) | Upgrade MapLibre GL JS to the latest release. | --- ## Full Minimal Example (HTML) ```html Soft Hillshade Example
``` Open the page, pan/rotate, and you should see a gentle, multi-directional hillshade that blends nicely with the satellite imagery underneath. --- ### TL;DR *Use a single `hillshade` layer with* ```json "hillshade-method": "multidirectional", "hillshade-exaggeration": 0.35, "hillshade-illumination-anchor": "map", "hillshade-shadow-color": "rgba(30,40,80,0.45)", "hillshade-highlight-color": "rgba(255,240,200,0.4)" ``` *and avoid stacking extra hillshade layers.* This removes the harsh black-and-white contrast while keeping performance optimal.
